Man soll aus diesen Punkten Gerade zusammensetzen, so dass mit Benutzung der geg. Winkel [-alle-] eine geg. ebene Geometrie wird d.h. alle Axiome erfüllt sind ausser dem Parallelenaxiom
english: It can also be expressed geometrically as follows: given are points, with directions through each point, and at these points angles between 2 given directions. One is to compose straight lines out of these points so that, using the given angles, a given plane geometry results, i.e. all axioms are satisfied except the parallel axiom.
topic: The page completes a remark on determining number fields with Hilbert's own methods, states the problem of mapping an arbitrary continuum onto the interior of a circle and gives a geometric reformulation, and reflects on the importance of number theory and geometric intuition for mathematicians.

triage.modern_statement: The note is a fragment. The lines before it pose an analytic problem: map an 'arbitrary continuum' onto the interior of a circle. This passage restates that problem in geometric terms. Take a 2-dimensional point set where each point has a set of directions and every pair of directions at a point has a given angle. In modern language, this extra data is close to an angle-measuring (conformal or infinitesimal metric) structure on a surface. The task is to choose a family of curves to serve as 'straight lines' so that, measuring angles with the given data, the result satisfies all of Hilbert's plane axioms except the parallel axiom, i.e. it is a neutral ('absolute') plane. Such planes are known to be Euclidean or Bolyai-Lobachevsky (hyperbolic), and hyperbolic geometry is usually modelled on the interior of a circle. So the most plausible reading is: show that the given surface with its angle structure can be identified with a disc model of hyperbolic geometry (or with the Euclidean plane). The fragment is too short to pin down the hypotheses exactly (what 'continuum' means, how smooth the angle data must be, whether the given angles must be kept exactly).
triage.answered_by: No definite identification. The closest documented results by Hilbert himself are (a) his 1902 paper 'Über die Grundlagen der Geometrie' (Göttinger Nachrichten / Math. Ann.), which shows that a plane with a continuous group of motions is Euclidean or Bolyai-Lobachevsky geometry, and (b) his 1903 'Neue Begründung der Bolyai-Lobatschefskijschen Geometrie' (Math. Ann. 57). A related published problem is Hilbert's 4th problem (geometries in which straight lines are shortest paths), studied by Hamel (1901) and finally solved by Pogorelov (1973). Another unverified possibility: if the given angles are read as a conformal structure, the 'map onto a circle's interior' wording resembles uniformization (Hilbert's 22nd problem, Koebe/Poincaré 1907). My searches did not confirm either link to this diary entry.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 1902 paper 'Ueber die Grundlagen der Geometrie' (Göttingen Nachrichten) argued that metric relations in a plane with a continuous group of motions correspond to Euclidean or Lobachevsky geometry. It is linked to Hilbert's 5th problem.
Hilbert, 'Neue Begründung der Bolyai-Lobatschefskijschen Geometrie', Math. Annalen 57 (1903), 137-150: Hilbert's axiomatic foundation of hyperbolic (non-parallel-axiom) plane geometry.
Hilbert's 4th problem asks for metrics in which the usual projective lines are geodesics. It was finally solved by A.V. Pogorelov (1973).
Hamel's 1901 Göttingen dissertation 'Über die Geometrien, in denen die Geraden die Kürzesten sind' was early work on Problem IV. Hilbert studied related geometries in the same period.

triage.why: The passage is a short reformulation of an analytic problem that is only partly visible on the page ('map an arbitrary continuum onto the interior of a circle'). Its wording is close to Hilbert's work of 1900-1903 on the foundations of geometry: neutral planes being Euclidean or hyperbolic, continuous motion groups, and the 4th problem on straight lines as shortest paths. A conformal-structure/uniformization reading is also possible. But none of the sources I found discusses this specific diary note, and the hypotheses are too vague to match it reliably to one published problem or solution.
